01

See the average after removing eligible low scores

The drop lowest grade calculator removes a chosen number of the smallest percentage scores, then averages the scores that remain. It is designed for a set in which every eligible score counts equally, such as a quiz category with a published rule allowing one quiz to be dropped.

A drop is a change to the set of records used in an average, not a bonus added to a mark. The excluded score disappears from both the sum and the count. This tool helps you check that arithmetic. It does not decide whether an assessment qualifies for a drop or whether a course actually offers the option.

02

Enter eligible percentages and a whole-number drop count

Enter percentage scores between zero and one hundred, separated by commas, spaces, or new lines. Decimal percentages are accepted. Include each eligible assessment once. The list can contain up to one thousand values, but it must contain at least one score.

Enter how many of the lowest scores should be removed. This must be a whole number and must leave at least one score in the list. Entering zero drops nothing and provides the ordinary equal-weight mean. Before using a nonzero count, check whether the policy excludes certain assessments from being dropped, requires attendance, or treats a missed submission differently from a completed low-scoring attempt.

03

Sort, remove, and average the retained grades

Adjusted average = Sum of retained percentage grades ÷ Number of retained grades.

The calculator orders the values from lowest to highest, removes the requested number from the low end, and applies the ordinary mean to the rest. It also reports the original average so you can compare the change.

For an equally weighted list, removing the smallest values cannot lower the average of the retained set. If every score is identical, dropping some of them leaves the mean unchanged. This property depends on equal weighting. Removing an assignment from a pooled-points category can behave differently because its point total changes both the earned and possible totals.

04

One dropped score changes the denominator too

Consider scores of 60%, 80%, 90%, and 100%. Their sum is 330, so the original average is 330 ÷ 4 = 82.5%. Dropping the lowest score removes sixty from the sum and one from the count. The retained mean is 270 ÷ 3 = 90%.

It would be incorrect to subtract sixty and continue dividing by four; that would leave an extra zero-like contribution in the denominator. If the policy allows two drops, the retained scores would be 90% and 100%, averaging 95%. If only one drop is permitted, the two-drop result is merely a hypothetical comparison and must not be presented as the official category average.

You can verify the one-drop change without changing any retained score: eighty plus ninety plus one hundred remains 270. The higher average comes entirely from excluding the lower value and recalculating the count, rather than improving those three marks.

05

Repeated grades and recorded zeroes

Suppose the list is 50%, 50%, 80%, and 100%, and one score is dropped. Either fifty can be removed because both have the same value. The remaining sum is 230 over three scores, producing about 76.67%. The calculator need not choose which assessment name belongs to the removed value.

A recorded zero is a valid percentage and will be among the lowest values. If zero, seventy, eighty, and ninety are eligible and one score is dropped, the retained average is 80%. That does not mean every zero can legally be excluded. A policy may require that an assessment was attempted or prohibit dropping a particular compulsory task.

06

Translate category changes into course changes carefully

The displayed result is the average of the retained list, not necessarily the full course grade. If the list represents a quiz category worth 20% of the course, moving its average from 82.5% to 90% increases its course contribution from 16.5 to eighteen percentage points.

That is a 1.5-point course increase, although the category average increased by 7.5 points. Keep the category weight separate from its internal drop rule. After finding the adjusted category mean, enter that mean and the category's proper course weight in the weighted grade calculator alongside the other categories. Do not also enter the individual quizzes there and count the same work twice.

07

Know when lowest percentage is not the right selection

In a pooled-points category, dropping the lowest percentage does not necessarily produce the best final ratio. For example, an assessment worth ten marks and an exam worth one hundred marks have different influence. This interface intentionally does not search for the most beneficial point-based exclusion.

Do not mix protected assessments with droppable ones and assume the smallest numerical value is eligible. Keep the policy's allowed set clear. If protected scores must remain in the same final average, perform a separate calculation that retains them and excludes only eligible records. Likewise, do not include future ungraded assignments as zeroes just to preview a drop; that can identify the wrong score for removal.

08

Use the comparison without depending on a future drop

Compare the original and adjusted means to understand the value of the published rule. Then focus on the topics behind lower results. A higher retained mean may make a grade look stronger while leaving the same knowledge gaps for a later cumulative examination.

As new assessments arrive, replace scenarios with actual marks and recalculate the whole eligible set. A newly earned low score can change which earlier result is removed. Keep the permitted drop count fixed unless the instructor changes the rule. If no scores remain after an attempted drop, there is no meaningful average; reduce the count or obtain clarification rather than treating an empty category as one hundred percent.

Quick answers

Frequently asked questions

What happens if I choose zero drops?

Every entered grade remains in the set. The adjusted result equals the ordinary arithmetic mean, which can be a useful baseline before comparing the effect of the drop count your course actually permits.

Can every grade be dropped?

No. At least one retained value is necessary to define an average. The calculator rejects a drop count equal to or greater than the number of scores, rather than inventing a result for an empty set.

Does the tool choose an assessment when low values tie?

It removes the necessary number of equal values. For this equal-weight numerical model, choosing one tied assessment over another does not change the mean. Administrative eligibility still depends on the actual assignment records.

Is this a reason to skip the next quiz?

No. The arithmetic cannot determine attendance obligations, drop eligibility, missed-work consequences, or how later scores will change the retained set. Use the result to understand a policy, and confirm those rules before making submission decisions.
